Daniel’s leap from “there exists an exact boundary condition” to “a human will never answer” quietly swaps a mathematical existence result for a physical/psychological inevitability. In the dice case, “standing on its edge forever” is an unstable equilibrium: it can exist in an idealized, perfectly deterministic model, yet it is destroyed by arbitrarily small perturbations (air molecules, table vibrations, numerical noise). That distinction matters because the set of initial conditions that produce the knife-edge behavior is typically measure-zero; it’s a separator between basins of attraction, not a robust outcome. Calling that “bifurcation” blurs the standard meaning in dynamical systems, where a bifurcation is a qualitative change in attractors as a parameter varies, not merely the existence of a decision boundary. A more precise framing would be “a discontinuous classifier applied to a continuous state induces decision boundaries,” which is true but weaker than the dramatic conclusion.

The human example then inherits an additional hidden assumption: that the input→decision map is continuous, deterministic, and must terminate in finite time for all non-boundary inputs. Real decision-making is not like a noiseless comparator; it is noisy, history-dependent, and time-bounded. In the mainstream modeling tradition (e.g., drift–diffusion and related sequential sampling models), indifference points predict *longer reaction times*, not infinite ones, precisely because internal noise almost surely breaks ties eventually; if you force a decision by deadline, you get random guessing near the boundary rather than non-termination ([Diffusion model](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drift-diffusion_model)). If Daniel’s claim relies on a strictly continuous deterministic brain with no noise and no deadlines, that premise is doing all the work—and it’s not “physical rules are continuous” so much as “the system is perfectly deterministic and tie-breaking is forbidden,” which is a different (and much stronger) stipulation.

Finally, labeling the constructed indifference case a “cognitohazard” seems rhetorically clever but conceptually mismatched. A hazard is typically robust to small perturbations; Daniel’s “exact interval” is, by his own logic, a knife-edge condition that vanishes under tiny timing jitter, attention fluctuation, or any socially normal escape hatch (“I don’t know,” “3,” “2,” silence, refusal). What Daniel has rediscovered is closer to the old philosophical problem of *Buridan’s ass*—a rational agent stuck between indistinguishable options—except that in both philosophy and engineering, the standard resolution is to add tie-breakers, noise, or costs for delay rather than to treat indecision as madness ([Buridan’s ass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buridan%27s_ass)). If the post is aiming at a broader point about how crisp categories sit atop continuous reality, it would land more sharply by emphasizing the *fragility* of the boundary and the practical mechanisms (noise, heuristics, deadlines) that prevent “infinite hesitation” in real systems.
